New guy here, and I'm ready to try the linux switch again. I've had dual boot setups before and always ended up needing windows-only software often enough to quit.

I use an old Clevo laptop that only takes one drive. Ideally I could dual-boot with 7 and have both encrypted, but in reality I'm a married engineer and I don't even torrent so I don't need encryption.

The problem I have with Linux, besides having a rare computer to start with, is that I want to interface with various chip programmers and serial adaptors. I have a windows work computer but I have no admin rights on it so I can't use any software we don't use at work- which limits me to a few really expensive chip programmers.

I don't really care for Ubuntu and I've heard rumors that it has windows-like telemetry. If it's truly the only option I'll try it again.

Linux-compatible hardware and software suggestions for cheap and flexible interface to a wide variety of ROM devices are also welcome. Worst case I can throw a bunch of those little arduino like devices at the problem and make my own reader/writer for each device I encounter. I'm currently trying to learn more about assembly by examining and slightly modifying devices I own that aren't open source. Sounds silly maybe, but that is how I learn best.
Embedded devs or other with unusual hardware, what's your favorite distro?

chip programmers on Linux is severally lacking. Flashrom.org supports a dozen or so options. Bus-pirate at http://dangerousprototypes.com will program many chips with i2c or spi interface only. Beyond that it requires a commercial programmer that almost always uses Windows software.
For operating a chip programmer, I just have a copy of XP in Virtualbox. VBox has USB support so it works most of the time.
Gentoo. It's incredibly easy to setup crossdev, and run/compile any software out there, even one that is alien to the distro.

This is the one where you compile your own, right? Let's say it took me all weekend to get GRUB and Arch installed slightly wrong but working with absolutely nothing installed, because all I had was the documentation and I don't know enough about Linux to know what's not mentioned.

Is it like a 2 weekend project? If I install it slightly wrong can I fix it or is it a nuke and start over situation?

Yes, it's that one. I've "learned" it after using debian for about 4 years, but that was about 2004? It's not a 2 weekend project, but the cool thing is that once you understand it, you understand how every distro works. It's a bit easier than it used to be too.

You should NEVER nuke an installation, unless you're not interested in learning what you did wrong. That said if you want stuff to just install and work you're probably better off with something else. Gentoo is all about learning by deconstruction.
